slides.title: TwinOps and team HackSmith
slides.alt: TwinOps is a rehearsal space for network repairs, created by team HackSmith.
paragraphs: TwinOps lets AI test a network repair in a separate network before an engineer decides what to apply.
Team HackSmith: Prabhakar Srivastava (leader) and Shivam Anand. Theme: Future of Work & Enterprise Productivity. The working prototype uses synthetic network scenarios.

slides.title: The problem and the idea
slides.alt: Metro screenshot shows failed return routes from Berlin and Hamburg through router B17.
paragraphs: Two branch sites lose access to an application. An engineer needs to restore service, but a quick rollback could break another connection.
A digital twin is a separate copy of the affected network. TwinOps lets AI test competing repairs there, then gives the engineer evidence before asking for approval.

Metro is the synthetic application network used in this prototype. A journey means a site-to-service connectivity check. In this actual recorded incident, Berlin and Hamburg fail while Munich and Frankfurt remain healthy.

slides.title: Where TwinOps fits
slides.alt: Diagram: network symptoms feed TwinOps experiments, followed by engineer review, approved change and recovery checks.
paragraphs: TwinOps sits between an incident and an approved network change. It reads symptoms from the target, rehearses candidate repairs in an isolated twin and sends measured evidence to an engineer.
The engineer reviews that evidence before authorizing a write to the target. Fresh checks then verify the outcome.
The distinction is that restoring access alone is insufficient. The selected change must also survive additional checks, with the exact diff and rehearsed rollback available in one reviewable record.

slides.title: Why one repair passes
slides.alt: Comparison: one bad route-rule removal and a full rollback both restore access, but the full rollback fails IPv6.
paragraphs: Gemini proposes candidate repairs. Twin experiments and fixed policy checks determine which proposals can proceed.
In the recorded run, removing one bad route rule restored access and passed the IPv6 check. Rolling back the full configuration also restored initial access, but failed IPv6 and stopped.
The workbench retains failed alternatives, the selected diff and rehearsed rollback. The editable slide table summarizes two of the five tested candidates and revisions.

slides.title: The complete incident flow
slides.alt: Eight-step diagram from observation through investigation, reproduction, comparison, challenge, review, approval and verified apply.
paragraphs: 1. Observe: Metro reports two failed journeys. 2. Investigate: Gemini ranks possible causes from the observations. 3. Reproduce: TwinOps copies the affected slice into its separate twin. 4. Compare: candidate repairs run against fresh copies of the faulty state.

5. Challenge: additional checks test for regressions. 6. Review: the engineer inspects the diff and rollback evidence. 7. Approve: approval binds to the exact tested change and target state. 8. Apply and verify: the gateway rechecks freshness and drift, applies the authorized change and checks recovery.

The top row runs left to right and the bottom row returns right to left. During steps 1–5, experiments stay on the twin. Missing evidence blocks a proposal. A failed apply or recovery check triggers rollback handling and escalation.

slides.title: The human approval decision
slides.alt: Enlarged workbench screenshot shows the exact change, tested state, rollback and conditions outside twin coverage.
paragraphs: The engineer approves a specific tested change: remove route-filter rule 30 from router B17. The review shows the change hash, target-state hash and rollback rehearsal.
The same panel explains untested conditions, including physical hardware and production-scale behavior. Passing technical tests alone does not authorize a network change.

This is a cropped screenshot from the actual hosted recording on 15 October 2026. The private credential form is outside the crop. The current public demo requires no passcode: its disabled field contains only placeholder dots. Human review and explicit approval are still required.

slides.title: Deployment architecture
slides.alt: Architecture diagram separates Vertex AI, the browser, Cloud Run, the Metro network, the digital twin and the authorized apply gateway.
paragraphs: The engineer uses the React workbench. Inside Cloud Run, the FastAPI orchestrator reads Metro observations and exchanges structured requests with Gemini 2.5 Flash through Vertex AI.

Metro and the digital twin use separate Linux network namespaces. The twin runs repair experiments and returns measured evidence. Fixed Proof Gate checks and human approval control the apply gateway. The model cannot directly write to the target network.

FRR, CoreDNS and nginx exercise routing, DNS and TLS. SQLite stores evidence on the instance. Secret Manager supplies credentials. Cloud Build and Artifact Registry build and deliver the container. Evidence and lab state are currently ephemeral.

slides.title: Technologies in the prototype
slides.alt: Table lists Google Cloud services and application components with their implemented responsibilities.
paragraphs: Cloud Run (second generation) hosts TwinOps, Metro and the isolated namespace networks. Gemini 2.5 Flash through Vertex AI supplies hypotheses, repair proposals, challenges and bounded revisions. The Google Gen AI SDK sends structured requests that undergo schema and action-catalogue validation.

Secret Manager stores the server credential for protected approval mode; public demo approval does not use it. Cloud Build and Artifact Registry build and store the container. React provides the review interface, FastAPI orchestrates investigations, and SQLite journals local evidence.

FRR, CoreDNS and nginx supply real routing, DNS, IPv4/IPv6 and TLS behavior. Firebase and Firestore are not used. The organizer clarification supplied by the project owner accepts the Cloud Run deployment path.

slides.title: Independent recovery evidence
slides.alt: Actual Metro screenshot compares all four journeys before, during and after the repair.
paragraphs: Two journeys failed, one route rule was removed, and all four journeys were healthy afterward. Metro probes the network independently of the planner.
The screenshot shows Berlin and Hamburg failing during the incident and recovering after the approved repair. Munich and Frankfurt remain healthy. The planner does not score its own success.
These results come from one actual hosted run on 15 October 2026. Sites and customer counts are synthetic. The displayed timings are illustrative and do not establish a latency improvement.

slides.title: Evidence and benchmarking
slides.alt: Table separates one hosted Gemini repair from a separate 320-case deterministic evaluation.
paragraphs: The hosted Gemini repair on 15 October 2026 used 10 actual model calls, no fallbacks and no diagnosis writes. It recorded five experiments, 13 challenges and 79 probes. All 11 post-change checks passed in each of three observation windows.

A separate deterministic evaluation on 13 October covered 320 cases: 200 verified repairs and 120 abstentions, with zero unsafe passes and all 13 controls passing. That suite uses a deterministic model twin and makes zero Gemini calls.
These evidence scopes are separate. Production reliability and operator time savings still need their own evaluation. The edited demonstration video is not a repair-time benchmark.

slides.title: Limits and next steps
slides.alt: Roadmap moves from the shared lab to operator evaluation, a read-only shadow pilot and operational hardening.
paragraphs: Today, the prototype supports routing, DNS and TLS exercises on synthetic topology. It uses one shared lab instance, ephemeral evidence and open demo approval with an unverified operator label.

Next, evaluate operator investigation and review effort against a baseline, measuring escalation, rollback outcomes and decision quality. Then validate adapters and twin coverage in a read-only shadow pilot before enabling operational changes.
Wider deployment needs durable evidence storage, individual identity, isolation per target, monitoring ownership and tested recovery. These are planned capabilities.
